title: How to read a Church document
hook: constitutions, encyclicals, exhortations: different weights, all cited by numbered paragraphs
tomorrow: how does a council picture God talking to people?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the classics with a shelf of five books, chosen for the hard night, not for the guests. The line was five books.

A homily mentions Lumen Gentium 11. A news story quotes a pope's encyclical, paragraph something. A parish bulletin cites an exhortation. No page numbers, no chapters: just a Latin name and a small number, as if every copy on earth were the same book. For the next stretch of days, this path opens the Church's own documents and reads them a few lines at a time. First, the puzzle of how to find your way around one.
screen: `A LATIN NAME AND A SMALL NUMBER.` → `NO PAGE, NO CHAPTER.` → `HOW DO YOU FIND YOUR WAY?`

segments.voice: Start with the kinds. A constitution is a council's own teaching document, and the bishops of the Second Vatican Council called some of theirs dogmatic constitutions, which marks them as weighty: Dei Verbum, on God's word, and Lumen Gentium, on the Church. An encyclical is a letter from a pope, addressed to the bishops and often to the whole Church, sometimes to everyone of good will. An exhortation is often written after a meeting of bishops, gathering up what was said and urging the Church on. Different kinds, different weights, and Catholic teaching takes those weights seriously. Next, the names. Each document is known by its opening words in Latin. Dei Verbum begins with the words for the word of God. Lumen Gentium begins with the light of the nations. So the name is a doorway: it tells you where the writer chose to start. Then the numbers, and here's the answer to the puzzle. These documents are divided into short numbered paragraphs, so anyone in any language can point to the same spot. Say Lumen Gentium 11 in a parish in Lagos or a classroom in Lima, and everyone lands on the same lines, whatever the page. That's how they'll be read here: one numbered paragraph at a time.
screen: `CONSTITUTION, ENCYCLICAL, EXHORTATION.` · `DIFFERENT KINDS, DIFFERENT WEIGHTS.` · `NAMED BY THEIR FIRST LATIN WORDS.` · `NUMBERED PARAGRAPHS, EVERY LANGUAGE.` · then, large: `NUMBERED PARAGRAPHS.`

segments.voice: If a phone is close, look up Dei Verbum and find the small number one at the start of the first paragraph. Read only that paragraph, slowly, once. If no phone is near, sit with the two opening words, the word of God, and let them be the doorway into the quiet.
Encyclical. A letter from a pope, sent to the bishops, the Church, and sometimes everyone of good will. Today's word.
Your line: numbered paragraphs. Small numbers that let a whole Church read the same lines together. A new block begins.

chat.says: want to quote a pope in my speech. found two versions online, different words. which one's real?
options: Maybe both. Translations differ; the paragraph number is the same in every language.
Whichever has a page number. The first printed edition is the only real one.
Neither. Popes write only in Latin, so every English version is made up.
chat.meaning: Church documents are divided into numbered paragraphs, so anyone in any language can point to the same spot, even when translations word it differently.

Lumen Gentium.meaning: Vatican II's constitution on the Church; Latin for light of the nations

Dei Verbum.meaning: Vatican II's constitution on God's word; Latin for the word of God

exhortation.meaning: a document urging the Church on, often after a meeting of bishops

Second Vatican Council.meaning: a worldwide council of Catholic bishops, often called Vatican II
